blockers.message: the review record has no `## code.review` section, while roles were active at it
R-skeptic-1 (The merge rests on "one e-mail = one person", which the design's own context contradicts) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it
R-skeptic-2 (Losing records are deleted with no way back) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it

findings.evidence:
Since an e-mail address identifies exactly one person, the job groups
customers by lower-cased e-mail, keeps the oldest record of each group,
moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The load-bearing assumption is refuted three lines above it, in Context: "Business customers often share a purchasing mailbox (`orders@acme.example`) between several buyers, each with their own customer record and billing address." Scenario: two buyers at Acme check out with `orders@acme.example`; the job keeps the older record, moves the second buyer's orders onto it and deletes the second buyer's record, so their name and billing address are lost and their orders are now attributed to another person. Pick a merge key that does not collapse distinct people (e.g. e-mail plus name and billing address, or e-mail only for guest records with matching identity fields), or exclude shared mailboxes explicitly; then add a spec scenario "two customers share an e-mail but have different names / billing addresses → both records remain", covered by a test in tasks.md. Reconsider the rejected alternative ("matching on name and address") with this case in mind — the design gives no reason for rejecting it.
findings.title: The merge rests on "one e-mail = one person", which the design's own context contradicts

findings.evidence: moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The merge is a one-way door: once a record is deleted, its name, billing address and created_at are gone, and the orders' original customer_id is overwritten. Any wrong merge (see R-skeptic-1) cannot be undone. The design has no Risks / Trade-offs or Migration Plan section and states no rollback. Keep the merged-away records recoverable (soft-delete or a merge log recording the old customer_id of each moved order and the deleted row), and/or run a dry-run report before the first destructive run; add a task that verifies a merge can be reverted.
findings.title: Losing records are deleted with no way back

findings.evidence: A nightly job SHALL merge customer records that share an e-mail address into the oldest one, moving their orders to it.
findings.recommendation: The design groups by "lower-cased e-mail", but the requirement does not say whether `Ada@Example.org` and `ada@example.org` "share an e-mail address", so the case-folding behavior cannot be checked against the spec. The only scenarios are "Two records, one e-mail" and "No duplicate": add edge cases for differing case / surrounding whitespace, a group of three or more records (which one survives, all orders moved), and records with the same created_at (tie-break for "the oldest one").
findings.title: The spec covers only the happy path and leaves "share an e-mail address" undefined

findings.recommendation: What Changes adds "A nightly job merges customers that share an e-mail address." — a scheduled component someone must run, observe and be able to stop, and which rewrites existing rows. The operations box is unticked with no reason, so the ops expert never reviews scheduling, failure reporting or how to switch the job off. Tick operations (and consider migration, since the job rewrites and deletes existing data), or state on the line why it does not apply.
findings.title: A new nightly job is deployed with operations unticked and no reason

findings.recommendation: The proposal ticks "personal-data — the job merges and deletes customer records", yet the change disables the privacy role, so the one domain the plan itself flags is reviewed by nobody (no review of erasure, retention, or attributing one person's orders and data to another). Remove the `privacy: never` override, or record who decided it and why.
findings.title: The privacy role is disabled for a change that merges and deletes personal data

findings.evidence: Guest checkouts create a new customer each time; support sees five records for one person.
findings.recommendation: The Why names the cause — `guest_checkout` in app/checkout.py inserts a new customer on every order — but the plan only cleans up afterwards, so support still sees duplicates for orders placed since the last run. The design does not weigh reusing a matching customer at checkout. Say why a nightly merge is preferred, or note it as a follow-up.
findings.title: A nightly clean-up leaves the cause of the duplicates in place
